title: Ang 74–78: the watches of the night
hook: life as four watches of the night
tomorrow: why would a book of hymns hold a ballad?

segments.voice: Yesterday, from ang 53 on: truth, lived. On ang 62, truth is high, and truthful living higher still. Now a hymn that tells time.

Wake up at three in the morning and the night has its own seasons: the early stretch where sleep came easy, the dead middle, the gray hour before the birds. Guru Nanak takes a night like that and lays a whole life across it. On ang 74, one human life fits inside the watches of a single night. And readers have never quite agreed on how to hear it.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `A LIFE INSIDE ONE NIGHT.` → `HOW DO YOU HEAR IT?`

segments.voice: The hymn is called Pahire, the watches, and it speaks to a vanjaria mitra, a merchant friend: someone who came here to trade. In paraphrase: in the first watch of the night, by the Order, you were placed in the womb. In the second, you were passed from arm to arm and played with, and forgot why you came. In the third, your mind was on wealth and youth. In the fourth, the reaper comes to the field. Now the two readings. Some hear an alarm. The night is shorter than you think, the merchant is spending it on the wrong goods, and the fourth watch arrives whether you're ready or not. On their side: the hymn really does end in the field. Others hear an invitation. Every watch is spoken to a friend, and the hymn keeps turning back to the Name, so no watch is too early or too late to remember why you came. On their side: you don't keep writing to a friend you've given up on. The two readings agree on the trade itself. A life is time, spent like money, and the hymn names what's worth buying with it.
screen: `A MERCHANT FRIEND, CAME TO TRADE.` · `WOMB, PLAY, WEALTH, THE REAPER.` · `READING ONE: AN ALARM.` · `READING TWO: AN INVITATION.` · then, large: `THE FOUR WATCHES.`

segments.voice: If you can, read the first watch on ang 74 before you start. Glance at the time on a clock or your phone and let it stand for the watch you're in, without judging it. Then close your eyes, and each time your mind wanders off to trade, let one word bring it back: the Name, or simply, the One.
Ang 74. The page where Guru Nanak's Pahire begins: a whole life laid across one night.
Carry it out the door: the four watches, and whichever one you're in is still yours. Goodnight, or good morning.

howItsDone: Sikhs reading the Granth in order reach the Pahire hymns in Sri Rag; they are also sung in kirtan, and some families recite them when reflecting on a life, at an anniversary or after a death.
